"Mummy, Papa, can I show you something?" Amandeep laid a printed timetable and three mock test sheets on the dining table.

Papa frowned. "What is this?"

"My week. Five coaching batches, school, travel. There's no time to practise what I learn. And look," Amandeep tapped the sheets. "Chemistry batch: my scores went 58, 57, 58. No change."

Mummy picked up the sheet. "So you want to quit?"

"Not quit. Drop the chemistry batch for two months. Use those hours for self-practice. If my chemistry score isn't above 65 by the December mock, I'll rejoin."

Papa was quiet. "Your cousin Jyoti did the same thing, didn't she?"

"Her scores went up."

"Two months," Papa said finally. "And we look at December together."

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt when Papa frowned at the papers?
qa.a: Amandeep was probably nervous about being refused, but prepared, having brought the timetable and the scores.

qa.q: What else could Amandeep offer to make the trial easier for the parents?
qa.a: Amandeep could share a weekly self-practice log with them, so they see how the freed hours are used.

qa.q: How does the proposal look to Papa by the end?
qa.a: Papa seems cautious but reassured, agreeing because there is a clear time limit and a mark to check in December.

grounding: Shows a student bringing the timetable and test results to parents, proposing to drop one batch for two months as a trial with clear marks targets.

subtype: Approach: negotiating a reduced load with parents [Action]
passage:
In January I was in four coaching batches, and I was drowning. I'm Saurabh, and I knew complaining wouldn't work with my parents. They'd paid the fees. They thought more classes meant more marks.

So my friend Arnab helped me prepare like it was a case. I printed my weekly timetable, 64 hours with travel. I brought my last four maths mock scores from the weekend batch: they hadn't moved. And my physics ones, from the batch I liked: rising.

At dinner, I laid it out. "I don't want to stop. I want to drop the weekend maths batch for two months. Use that time to solve problems. If I'm not above 70 in maths by March, I'll go back."

My father went quiet. My mother asked, "And who checks?"

"We all do. March mock, together."

They agreed. By March I had 74.

qa.q: What were Saurabh's weekly hours with travel?
How did Saurabh feel before the dinner conversation?
qa.a: Saurabh felt overwhelmed, like drowning, and doubtful that complaining would convince the parents.

qa.q: What else could Saurabh have included to strengthen the case?
qa.a: Saurabh could have shown a sample weekly plan for the freed hours, so the parents could see exactly how the time would be used.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's mother see the agreement?
qa.a: Saurabh's mother seems cautious but willing; asking who checks shows a wish for a clear way to review the decision.

grounding: A reflective account of a student bringing a timetable and test scores to parents and proposing to drop a batch for two months as a trial with a marks target.
